History:
• 40-year-old woman presents with progressive left-sided hearing difficulty and constant numbness over the left jaw/ear region.  
• Onset: ≈3 weeks ago; symptoms have persisted without improvement.  
• Laterality: exclusively left.  
• Associated symptoms: intermittent left-sided tinnitus; brief dizziness when tinnitus occurs.  
• Denies ear pain, discharge, itching, fever, limb weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, or visual changes.  
• No recent trauma.  
• Concerned about seriousness of condition; seeks reassurance.

Past Medical History:
• Nasal polyps (uses intranasal spray PRN; name unknown).  
• Remote “labyrinthitis” (details/date not provided).  
• Allergies: Latex.  
• Medications:  
  – Intranasal spray for nasal polyps, dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – OTC Rennie (antacid), dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Family history: Brother with neurofibromatosis.  
• Social: Professional jockey; lives with partner; no pets. Tobacco/alcohol/substance use not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Tele-visit only; no vitals or in-person findings recorded.  
• Patient reports intact speech and swallowing; appears alert and conversant.  
• Objective cranial-nerve, otoscopic, and neurologic exams: Not recorded.

Impression:
Unilateral left-sided sensorineural symptoms with facial numbness—needs in-person evaluation.  
Top working diagnoses (consistent with transcript):  
1. Idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis (Bell’s palsy) – suggested by clinician; would explain facial sensory change, usually benign.  
2. Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) – progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, facial numbness; supported by family history of neurofibromatosis.  
3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome – less likely; pain/rash absent.

Management Plan:
• Arrange same-day face-to-face GP/neurological examination for full cranial-nerve and otoscopic assessment.  
• Admin team to book Central London clinic appointment; patient to phone support line in ~5 min to confirm slot.  
• Reassured patient that condition unlikely to be life-threatening but requires prompt examination.  
• No medications initiated today.  
• Safety-net advice: if sudden worsening of hearing, new facial weakness, severe dizziness, headache, or vision change occur before appointment, seek emergency care.

Patient Summary:
40-year-old woman with 3-week history of left-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, and facial numbness. No red-flag neurologic deficits on history. Needs in-person cranial-nerve/ear exam today to confirm suspected Bell’s palsy or other etiology.

Key Takeaways:
• Attend same-day clinic visit for full examination.  
• Call support team within 5 minutes to arrange appointment.  
• Seek urgent care if symptoms acutely worsen.

Next Steps:
• Complete neurological and otoscopic exam today.  
• Consider audiometry and MRI internal auditory canal/C-P angle if examination suggests sensorineural deficit or facial-nerve involvement.  
• Follow-up after examination to discuss findings and management (e.g., steroids for Bell’s palsy or ENT/neuro referral if tumor suspected).

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing: vitals, objective ear/neurologic exam, comprehensive medication list, smoking/alcohol history.  
• Transcript vs DDx conflicts: clinician leans toward Bell’s palsy whereas DDx ranks vestibular schwannoma higher—no definitive conflict; diagnosis pending examination.  
• Transcript quality: clear audio; no major inaudible sections.
